meaning: The shared roster in the system home.
Builds the database and installs workspaces. Builds and checks pages.
The clock that starts scheduled work.
A trigger during a runtime session.
A pack with its own tables, command, and templates.
Outside material kept as source evidence.
The rules that name the source and writer for a fact.
A row, a system trail, and a workspace report.
The tables and naming rules.
A procedure an agent follows for a task.
The agent and workshop that keep the skills.
The page an agent reads at the start.
The installed Foxrun code, shared settings, and database.
Knowledge pages that cite outside material.
The library and default home of a capture.
The knowledge in Atlas and workspace wikis.
The folder that contains your workspaces.
Frozen work, handoffs, snapshots, and run reports.
Living pages, one per topic.
Pages that show the business from source rows.
Living pages for things being built.
The agents that work in one workspace.
The list that controls where skills apply.
The system parts every install includes.
The name chosen for the memory job.
Code reads an outside source and refreshes its mirror on a schedule. It ships with the add-on; the outside system owns the facts; implementations can change without changing tables.

An outside system owns these rows; a feeder refreshes them one way; local users never edit copied facts. Keep each outside ID and row age; keep local additions in a separate table linked to the mirror.
Presents views and trends for a person; it owns no data and is not a database type. Its skill generates it and records runs in history; keep an exact rendered page in `outputs/` when needed.
A kept reply in its own frozen file.
Holds rows that Person and authorized agents write and edit. The local writer accepts field changes under their rules; other surfaces submit requests.
Holds dated observations that a schedule appends and nobody changes. Its writer adds rows with an `as_of` date to preserve values for comparison over time.
A moment that fires a command.

A saved database query reads existing rows; the database computes results without owning separate business data. Its module blueprint ships it; skills call it by name; agents propose it; Person approves it through shared creation.
A place for one business or body of work.

Directing work across agents and runtimes, retrieving results, and managing the lifecycle of delegated work. Native runtime paths and Herdr are possible adapters; neither defines the whole capability.
One lead runs several agents from one brief, then reviews and closes their work.

One identity on one runtime: a Hermes profile, a Claude subagent (`.claude/agents/*.md`), or a Codex custom agent (`.codex/agents/*.toml`). The same persona on two runtimes (e.g. the Keeper) is two agents that share a name.
Its own object, seven dimensions from the Anatomy of an Agent: model, contract, capabilities, stores, anchor, triggers, guardrails. Links to many Capability Records. ADR 0005.
One usable thing in eight categories: Skill, CLI, MCP, Plugin, Service, Connection, Hook, Script.

One object for everything an agent can use: type is skill, cli, mcp, plugin, or automation; trigger is on demand, event, or schedule; connection is a field naming the outside account. Service, hook, and script are all automation. ADR 0005.

Where an agent or capability belongs: Global (home-directory dotdirs) or one workspace. For Claude/Codex, scope is the literal location of the definition file; for Hermes, scope is the lane the profile's working directory points at.
The affected boundary on a decision, task link, or external system record.
Facts held as rows that authorized writers can change.
A collection is a named, marketable group of related object types inside a module. A folder or table that holds one object type is not a collection.
A portfolio contains workspaces and shared material. It sets the broadest scope in this model.
A workspace is a portable operating home for a business or another continuing body of work.
A function is a continuing seat of responsibility with an owner and a scorecard. It owns recurring work inside an organization.
A subfunction is a function with a parent. It adds no container type.
A kit is a module someone else built, used as it ships. Keep its native structure and names.
A subcollection is a collection with a parent collection.
A tier says which workspaces receive a module. The three tiers are base, workspace type, and add-on.

word: You install a module, you open a collection (rule)
meaning: You install a module. You open a collection.
An object type names a distinct thing the business tracks, with its own purpose and rules.
A supertype supplies shared fields and rules across distinct object types. It needs shared fields and a shared rule or query.
A subtype is an object type considered in relation to its supertype. This relationship describes the object, not nested placement.
A link connects related records or files.
Playbooks explain how work must run. They always live in files, such as skills, procedures, and agent rules.
Records hold changing business state. A linked file can hold the readable body while the row owns current state.
History preserves what happened or what was kept at a particular time. It uses frozen files or rows.

word: A file that claims a status is wrong (rule)
meaning: The database owns current state; a file holds the body or evidence. Generated reports display state from views without owning it.
JSONL stores one JSON record per line. Exported state is a copy; the local database remains authoritative.
A table holds rows that the person and authorized agents write and edit. The local writer accepts changes under the rules for each field.
A mirror holds a local copy of rows that an outside system owns. The feeder refreshes those rows; local users never edit the copied facts.
A trend holds dated observations that a schedule appends and nobody changes. These rows preserve values for comparison over time.
A view is a saved database query that reads existing rows without owning separate business data. The database computes its result.
A report presents views and trends for a person. It holds no data of its own and is not a database type.
A feeder is code that reads a source and refreshes its mirror on a schedule. The feeder writes the mirror rows; the outside system owns their facts.
A contract defines rules an agent must follow. Business agreements use agreement, whose row links the draft or signed document.
A template is a reusable file that supplies a starting shape for its user's output. It travels with the skill or module that uses it.
A decision records a choice, its reason, and its current standing. Its row holds state, scope, date, and what it replaces.
An approval records the person's response to an exact version of something. Approval does not prove sending, external acceptance, delivery, or payment.
Activity records who changed a record, what changed, when, and from where. Every accepted change leaves an append-only row.
A tag names an approved subject shared by related material. Approved tags live as rows, with one list per workspace.
A topic is the subject that material is about. Its wiki page gathers tagged material across object types in date order.
The topic rule lets the person name the subject while the agent chooses the correct object type. A choice becomes a decision row; a to-do becomes a task row.
A workspace type names the business domain that determines its shared module needs. The workspace-type tier adds to base.
A program is a large, coordinated effort with one record that everyone reads and updates.
A work stream is a project that belongs to a program; the same table holds both. A standalone row in that table is called a project.
A project delivers a defined result and always ends. Its row owns current state.
A Rock is a goal with horizon quarter. It needs no separate milestone object.
A task is one piece of work with an owner and a completion check. A task can stand alone.
A schedule defines when recurring work runs. It supplies the timing for a workflow or feeder.
A measure is a named number with an owner and target for a function or goal. The blueprint stores its definition in measures and dated observations in measure_history.
A scorecard groups measures so its owner can compare results with targets. A function uses its scorecard to track ongoing responsibility.
Replaces names the older record or decision that the current record replaces.
Backlog means the work is decided but not planned now.
To do means the work is next and has not started.
In progress means the work started but is not finished.
Blocked means the work cannot continue until a named condition changes.
A module is a group of tables in the core database. Every core table belongs to exactly one module.
A collection is a named, marketable group of related object types inside a module. A folder or table that holds one object type is not a collection.
Knowledge holds what is known. It may live in rows when agents query and cite it.
Each install has one core database, with every table once. Rows owned by a business carry a workspace column.
An organization is a people-module record. It is outside the work ladder.
A theme is a topic tag that can sit on anything. A program may use its topics as headlines to group work streams.
A goal is the why at the top of the work ladder. Measures and their dated observations judge it.
A subtask is a child row under a task, inside or outside a program. It has one parent and cannot have its own child.
A workflow is a YAML file that flow.py runs. Each workflow also has a short Markdown page that explains it in plain words.
A run is one job an agent or tool does. Its row is created at start and updated at end with status, result, and cost.
A standing task holds each day's run of purely recurring work. It is not a new task per day.
Replaced is the status of a record that a newer record replaces. The newer row stores the replaces link to the older row.
Done means the work is checked and nothing remains to ship. Finished work that is not yet checked or shipped is in-review.
